articles.title: Why Nepal is burying its flood victims instead of cremating them
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Nepal is a Hindu-majority country where cremation is the customary final rite for most Hindus. Yet after the devastating floods that swept through par.
articles.body: Nepal is a Hindu-majority country where cremation is the customary final rite for most Hindus. Yet after the devastating floods that swept through parts of the country, authorities have been burying unidentified bodies instead of cremating them. The reason is not a change in religious practice. It is a response to the large number of bodies being recovered, limited morgue space and the fact that many victims cannot yet be identified.Authorities are treating the burials as a temporary arrangement. Before a body is placed in the ground, officials are collecting DNA samples and recording identifying details so that families may still be able to locate and claim the remains later.According to The Statesman and various media reports, unidentified flood victims are being buried in Chitwan district after authorities collect DNA samples, assign identification codes and record the exact locations of their graves.Why are the bodies being buried?The scale of the disastrous floods has put Nepal's mortuaries under severe pressure. Bodies recovered from the floods were also beginning to decompose, making prolonged storage increasingly difficult. According to media reports, authorities were dealing with unidentified bodies at hospitals while freezing facilities were unable to accommodate all the remains. With the bodies decomposing, temporary burial became necessary.Morgues and mortuaries were overwhelmed by the number of bodies being brought in, leaving authorities with the difficult task of managing and preserving unidentified remains. The burials therefore do not mean that the victims' identities have been abandoned. Instead, authorities are trying to preserve enough information to identify them later.Each body is being given an identification numberThe bodies are not simply being placed in an anonymous mass grave. Authorities are creating records for the individual remains. According to The Statesman, each unidentified victim is assigned a unique identification code, while the burial location is recorded so the remains can be traced later. This creates a link between the remains and the records kept by the authorities. The burial sites are also being documented. Photographs and other records are being maintained, while GPS coordinates are being recorded for the graves. That means authorities can potentially locate a particular grave even after the burial has taken place.DNA is the key to identifying the deadDNA samples are being collected from unidentified bodies before burial. At the same time, relatives of people reported missing can provide their own DNA samples. The samples can then be compared with DNA taken from the recovered remains. DNA records are being preserved specifically to allow future identification if relatives come forward.The process is important because some bodies have been recovered far from where people went missing, while others are too badly decomposed or damaged to be identified through appearance alone.Officials are recording more than genetic material. According to various media, photographs, clothing, jewellery, tattoos and other identifying marks are also being documented. Nepal Police has also published details of some unidentified victims in an effort to help families searching for missing relatives.Why are the graves being prepared carefully?The burial arrangement is designed with future identification in mind. Burial pits are being dug around 1.5 metres deep, with about 40 cm of space left between bodies. The arrangement is intended to reduce the risk of DNA contamination and make future identification and exhumation possible.What happens if a victim is identified later?Identification does not end with the burial. If DNA testing establishes that a buried victim is the missing member of a family, officials can use the identification number and burial records to locate the remains. According to media reports, the remains can be handed over to the family once the victim has been identified. The family can then perform the funeral rites according to its traditions. This is why the burials are being handled differently from a conventional mass burial. Authorities are attempting to preserve the identity of every victim even when the person cannot be named immediately.The problem is bigger than the burial groundsThe decision to bury the unidentified bodies comes as Nepal continues to deal with a large number of missing people. Close to a thousand bodies have been recovered and thousands of people are still missing.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Building near an airport? Centre plans faster height clearances, local-level NOCs

articles.body: Securing a no objection certificate (NOC) for buildings near airports has been a complex hurdle for developers due to lengthy delays in height clearance by the Airports Authority of India (AAI).However, the Union civil aviation minister, Kinjarapu Rammohan Naidu, recently announced a series of targeted reforms to streamline and accelerate building height approvals.Under the existing setup, developers often finalised building designs and submitted housing plans without knowing the precise height clearance permitted for their specific plot. If aviation authorities later flagged the height as an obstacle, projects had to be redesigned from scratch, causing massive financial and time losses.Now, the ministry is moving toward a system that provides applicants with permissible building heights at the very initial stage of planning. Initially targeted at major metropolitan hubs such as Delhi, Mumbai, and Hyderabad, this approach allows housing societies, architects, and builders to design projects within approved vertical limits from day one.Currently, the no objection certificate application system (NOCAS) oversees height restrictions spanning a radius around airports up to 20 km for visual flight rules (VFR) and 56 km for instrument flight rules (IFR).To eliminate the need for every property owner to apply directly to the central aviation authority, the government is exploring decentralisation by empowering urban local bodies (ULBs) or municipal corporations to issue height NOCs at the local level based on pre-mapped aviation zoning data.Here, routine housing approvals can be integrated directly into regular municipal building plan sanctions.The new directive emphasises minimising initial physical site visits and rationalising document requirements. By leveraging automated digital tools, spatial mapping, and transparent public data, the approval process will rely far less on manual verification, drastically cutting down clearance timelines.The ministry has given a strict 15-day timeline to officials for finalisation and implementation of the reforms.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: US judge blocks Trump’s fresh bid to curb birthright citizenship: 'Children covered by earlier SC ruling remain US citizens at birth'
articles.summary: US News: A US district judge in Maryland has blocked President Donald Trump’s latest attempt to restrict birthright citizenship, saying the executive order (EO.
articles.body: A US district judge in Maryland has blocked President Donald Trump’s latest attempt to restrict birthright citizenship, saying the executive order (EO) cannot be enforced against children whose citizenship rights have already been recognised by the Supreme Court (SC) earlier.Judge Deborah L. Boardman on Wednesday issued a preliminary injunction against the EO issued by Trump in August. This EO sought to deny citizenship to certain US-born children based on the immigration status or activities of their parents.In her order, Judge Boardman pointed out that the Supreme Court had already settled the constitutional issue in its June ruling on Trump’s earlier attempt to restrict birthright citizenship. The Supreme Court had held that children born in the US to parents who are unlawfully or temporarily present are “citizens at birth.”Trump had issued his earlier EO seeking to restrict birthright citizenship on Jan 20, 2025, shortly after returning to the White House. The Supreme Court’s June ruling effectively invalidated that EO as unconstitutional.Judge Boardman’s order relates to a class-action case brought by CASA Inc and the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project and individual plaintiffs, “The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth,’” Judge Boardman stated. “Trump v/s Barbara (the SC order) is the law of the land. The President must follow it,” the order added.Trump’s EO issued last month, in August , had sought to create several categories in which federal agencies would not bestow citizenship to US-born children. These included cases where a parent was designated an ‘alien enemy’, worked for a foreign government or international organisation, or had engaged in a commercial transaction or fraud linked to obtaining birthright citizenship. This executive order was projected as a crackdown on birth-tourism.Judge Boardman, however, said the question before her was narrower than whether every provision of the EO issued in August was unconstitutional. She ruled that applying the executive order to the certified class was “almost certainly unconstitutional” because the Supreme Court had already determined that these children are citizens at birth.The judge also rejected the Trump administration's argument that the case was premature because government agencies had not yet issued detailed guidance on how the order would be implemented. She emphasised that loss of citizenship, even temporarily, could have cascading consequences and that the balance of equities and public interest favoured preventing confusion and upheaval.The ruling is another setback for the Trump administration's effort to narrow birthright citizenship. But immigration attorneys point out that it leaves open the possibility of further litigation over the scope of the executive order issued in August.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: El Niño is being 'supersized before our eyes,' U.N. warns. What that means for the weather where you live this fall and winter.
articles.summary: El Niño is expected to persist until February 2027, bringing risks of extreme weather.
articles.body:
El Niño is being "supersized before our eyes," and the world is in "the danger zone of extreme weather," the U.N. warned Thursday.

The latest data on the natural weather phenomenon indicates an "exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100%" that the current El Niño will continue until February 2027.

The more powerful an El Niño, the greater the likelihood that it will significantly shift rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide and fuel extreme weather. NOAA has previously warned of a 69% chance that this El Niño will be the strongest in the past 70 years.

El Niño officially formed in June and, according to the World Meteorological Organization, is expected to continue over the fall and winter. Its peak is projected to be toward the end of this year.

"The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement on the climate phenomenon Thursday.

"Sea surface temperatures are rising, temperatures keep climbing, and the world is in the danger zone of extreme weather. The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people. We must win that race."

"We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," added WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo.

In North America, El Niño tends to increase the likelihood of wetter conditions in the South, milder temperatures in the North and a quieter Atlantic hurricane season. Its most significant impact on U.S. weather is likely to emerge in the fall and peak during the winter.

What will this mean for the weather in the U.S.?

The severity of El Niño's impacts depends on where you live.

"El Niño tends to increase the storm track over the southern tier of the United States, increasing the chances of above-average precipitation," Michelle L'Heureux, a physical scientist at NOAA's Climate Prediction Center, told Yahoo News in August.

Broadly speaking, northern parts of the country could see warmer temperatures, while other regions may experience drier conditions.

L'Heureux said the southward shift in the storm track also leaves parts of the northern U.S. drier than normal and increases the likelihood of above-average temperatures.

A strong El Niño typically brings wetter and cooler-than-normal conditions from late fall through winter. Thunderstorm activity often increases along the Gulf Coast and in the lower Mississippi and Tennessee valleys. Spring and summer wildfire risk also tends to decrease across the Southeast.

El Niño often brings wetter-than-normal conditions, especially during midwinter, although the signal is less consistent than in the Southeast. Increased precipitation can also reduce spring and summer wildfire risk across parts of the Southwest, including the Great Basin and southern Rockies.

The Pacific Northwest and Northern Rockies

A strong or very strong El Niño typically brings milder conditions and below-normal snowfall as Pacific air limits the buildup of cold air over western and central Canada. Parts of the Rockies can receive above-normal snowfall, while the northern U.S. tends to be warmer and drier, increasing spring wildfire risk in the Northern Rockies.

Winters are often drier than average, particularly across the Ohio and Tennessee valleys. At the same time, El Niño can increase thunderstorm activity from the lower Mississippi Valley into the Tennessee Valley.

A strong El Niño generally brings a milder winter with below-normal snowfall across much of the region. Despite the warmer pattern, the risk of powerful coastal storms, including nor'easters, can still be elevated.

A strong or very strong El Niño typically strengthens the subtropical jet stream during the fall and winter, steering more storms across the southern U.S. and suppressing Atlantic hurricane activity, according to Steven DiMartino, chair of the American Meteorological Society's Board of Digital Meteorologists.

"While you only need one hurricane to have significant impacts, a very strong El Niño produces significant wind shear in the tropical Atlantic," he said. "That prevents most tropical waves from forming and threatening the U.S."

The biggest impacts from El Niño tend to occur in the winter months, though the effects may linger beyond the winter," Nat Johnson, a physical scientist at NOAA's Climate Prediction Center and lead of the El Niño Southern Oscillation team, told Yahoo News.

Johnson added that during the following spring and summer, El Niño can increase or reduce the wildfire risk depending on where you live.

Forecast models increasingly point to a powerful event. On Aug. 13, NOAA projected a 90% chance of El Niño reaching "very strong" status, giving it a 69% chance of being "a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950."

Scientists declare an El Niño has formed when temperatures in a key stretch of the central Pacific Ocean (known as "Niño 3.4") run 0.5°C above average for several consecutive months, according to NOAA.

If temperatures are 0.5°C above normal on average, an El Niño is considered weak; 1°C, moderate; 1.5°C, strong; and 2°C, very strong.

According to the WMO's findings released on Sept. 3, weekly sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region between late July and mid-August ranged from approximately 2.2°C to 2.6°C above average. In some areas, subsurface ocean temperatures were more than 8°C above average during July and early August, indicating continued intensification.

Berkeley Earth , a nonprofit climate research group, said in an analysis released Aug. 13 that it projected a peak near 4°C around November, which would make it the strongest El Niño in the observational record.

It also noted that July 2026 was provisionally the second-warmest July on record, with extreme weather events recorded worldwide."Extreme heat and wildfires affected much of the Northern Hemisphere. Western Europe recorded its hottest June–July period on record, with major wildfires across the Mediterranean, while Canada saw extensive wildfire activity," Berkeley Earth said.

Whether 2026 becomes the hottest year on record remains to be seen, but 2027 is far more likely to break the previous record. As Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather told the Associated Press in August, "It's going to keep getting worse."

"The current trends and developments support that this El Niño will surpass the 1997-98 and 2015-16 events, which are considered the strongest on record," DiMartino told Yahoo News. "Given that El Niño's peak is in late November, the potential to rise by as much as 3°C to 4°C is becoming increasingly likely."

articles.title: Orange Order submits new Drumcree parade plans
articles.summary: The organisation says the plans have been scaled back and it hoped the parade would be allowed along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road.
articles.body:
The Orange Order has announced plans for a "limited" parade at Drumcree, one of the most contentious parade routes in Northern Ireland.

It said the plans had been scaled back and it hoped the parade would be allowed along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road. Instead of 400 people and two bands taking part, only 60 members would march along the road in Portadown in silence on Sunday 27 September.

The submission comes after a court case saw the Parades Commission's most recent determination on Drumcree overturned .

At a press conference, the Orange Order said members of the Parades Commission had "no credibility" to adjudicate on their application and should resign.

The commission had banned this year's parade from entering the Garvaghy Road - a move which reflected every decision it has made since 1998.

In 1998, the Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road on the end leg of its annual march after a service at Drumcree Church.

It was a move that ultimately led to a decades-long parading dispute, sparking some of the most serious public disorder in Northern Ireland's history.

Stand-offs continued in subsequent years as members of the Order walked to police barricades in protest at the restrictions. Protests were also held by residents living along the Garvaghy Road.

The commission, which adjudicates on contentious parades in Northern Ireland, was heavily criticised by unionist politicians and the Orange Order after last month's court case.

High Court Judge Mr Justice McAlinden referred to "errors", "short cuts" and "sloppy procedures" in the approach of the commission to making its determination.

What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about?

Bryant orders independent review of Parades Commission

Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson said they had "lodged a notification to complete our return church parade, which we have been unlawfully and unjustly denied since 1998, and to bring our bannerette home to Carleton Street Orange Hall for the first time in just under 30 years".

He said the current Parades Commission should not be making the final determination on the submission, as a result of the recent court case.

"That this commission remains in office, particularly the chair, is an affront to good public administration and undermines the authority of the secretary of state, who has shown himself impotent in the face of belligerent and arrogant commission," he said.

"Let us be very clear: they have no credibility, they have no legitimacy and they have no lawful right to play any role in this determination."

He added that there was no threat of violence or disruption from "any section of our community" regardless of the outcome of the application.

Portadown deputy district master Alistair Power said: "This limited parade is proportionate, inoffensive and wholly reasonable.

After the court case, there were calls for the resignation of the commissioners, including the chair, Prof Evelyn Collins. One commissioner Billy Gamble, who had faced the most public criticism, resigned .

The five-member Parades Commission now has 24 days to make a decision.

They will consult widely before announcing their verdict.

The commissioners' jobs are part-time but their deliberations will be long and intensive.

The deadline for a decision is Sunday 27 September but it is likely to come a few days beforehand.

Anyone who disagrees with their judgement has the right to seek a judicial review of the decision.

A judge-led review into the Parades Commission is due to begin this month , instructed by the Secretary of State, Chris Bryant, and it will be completed before the end of November.

Dessie is a resident on the Garvaghy Road and and said the Orange Order was "marching over our rights".

Speaking to The Nolan Show, Dessie said there "should be no parade ever" on the Garvaghy Road.

Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, has criticised the plan.

"Stop playing politics, get real, go home," he said.

"What the Orange Order is trying to do is just increase tensions even further. Two of the political parties, the TUV and the DUP, who have been vocal on this are looking forward to next year's elections."

Posting on social media , First Minister Michelle O'Neill, said: "The days of unwanted marches being imposed on the Garvaghy Road community are over.

"The people of this small community should be left to live in peace, free from fear and intimidation," she added.

Jim Allister, leader of the Traditional Unionist Voice, said the arrangements for the planned parade were "very modest, very generous, very neighbourly".

Democratic Unionist MP Carla Lockhart, her party colleague Jonathan Buckley and loyalist activist Jamie Bryson, who is one of the order's legal advisers, were also present at the conference.

Bryson said the district had "a legal obligation to notify if they are going to have a parade and they have discharged their legal obligations as people who want to act within the law".

"They are entitled to do that as a matter of law and it is for those who oppose them and the commission to reach a very high threshold to justify any interference and on any analysis its very difficult to see how that threshold would be convincingly met for this notification," he added.

Speaking to Good Morning Ulster , leader of the opposition, Matthew O'Toole said the submission was an attempt to "revive a long dormant dispute over a parade".

"That is deeply irresponsible and concerning not just for the community in Portadown but for most people in Northern Ireland who want to have a shared peaceful and respectful future, this is an example of division from the past," he said.

"I don't think this is an example of someone trying to find a mediated or shared approach I think it's about trying to create divisions and spectacle."

Sinn Féin MLA John O'Dowd said the size of the march was "irrelevant" and that "nothing has changed" in what the Orange Order said at their press conference on Thursday.

"It's the same old agenda - an unwanted march on a community that has suffered greatly over many, many years, and who has now had the opportunity to live in peace and wants to continue to live in peace," he added.

High Court quashes decision to restrict annual Drumcree parade

articles.title: Mayor of London car tax conviction formally withdrawn
articles.summary: The conviction against Sir Sadiq Khan is withdrawn after he was prosecuted in a car ownership scam.
articles.body:
A car tax conviction against the Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan has been formally withdrawn after he was criminally prosecuted for not taxing a 24-year-old Nissan Micra he did not own.

The DVLA requested the withdrawal at Hereford Magistrates' Court on Thursday after the mayor's team said the conviction was the result of a "scam".

The Labour politician, 55, was found guilty of keeping an unlicensed vehicle by a magistrate last month in a criminal prosecution brought by the DVLA.

A spokesperson for the mayor said it was "not the first time" Khan had been victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that he was the owner of a vehicle.

At a hearing before magistrates at Hereford Justice Centre on Thursday, the case was formally reopened against the mayor and withdrawn by the panel after a request from the DVLA.

Neither the mayor nor a representative from the DVLA were present at the court for the one-minute hearing.

The legal advisor told the panel of magistrates they may be aware of the case as it was "widely publicised" on Wednesday, adding: "The DVLA have requested that the original matter, if you consider it to be reopened, be marked withdrawn."

Chairwoman of the bench Mrs Digings JP said: "We accept the reopening of the case as requested.

"Further to the request from the DVLA, we are going to mark the matter as withdrawn."

Last month, a magistrate sitting in a private hearing of the Single Justice Procedure in Herefordshire convicted Khan in his absence and ordered that he pay a £220 fine, £85 in costs and settle the £35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra.

Court documents showed letters regarding the unpaid road tax bill had been sent to Gordon Ramsay's east London restaurant instead of the mayor.

The DVLA said a letter asking for confirmation of the identity of the car owner, which was sent to the wrong address, went unanswered in January.

This led to a criminal prosecution on 18 August after no plea was entered to the charge.

The mayor's adviser said the DVLA would investigate the false registration of the car.

articles.title: Free travel pilot scheme for young people approved
articles.summary: The 29-week scheme for those aged five to 18 will run from February and is expected to cost £7.6m.
articles.body:
Children and young people who live in Sheffield will get free bus and tram travel across South Yorkshire after a pilot scheme was voted through by councillors.

Sheffield City Council's strategy and resources committee approved a 29-week scheme for people aged five to 18.

The trial will run from 15 February 2027 and is expected to cost £7.6m.

Council leader Fran Belbin said it would help families with the cost of living and give thousands of young people greater independence.

"The cost of a bus or tram journey should never be what stops a young person getting to college, taking up an apprenticeship, joining a sports club or simply spending time with friends," she said.

Belbin revealed the pilot has deliberately been timed to run until September 2027, when a separate scheme run by South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard will provide region-wide free travel scheme for the same age group.

The pilot has been developed with the South Yorkshire Mayoral Combined Authority, drawing on experience from Barnsley's MiCard scheme, which saw passenger numbers increase particularly in some of the most deprived areas.

Eligible children and young people will use a dedicated smartcard and usage, journey patterns, the cost and impact on the transport network will be monitored so the success of the pilot can be assessed.

articles.summary: US News: Vice President JD Vance’s mother, Beverly Vance Aikins, has hit out at Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed over his remarks about Vanc.
articles.body: Vice President JD Vance’s mother, Beverly Vance Aikins, has hit out at Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed over his remarks about Vance, his wife Usha, and their children, saying she would “probably punch” him if she ever met him.According to the New York Post, Aikins made the remarks during an interview with OutKick host Tomi Lahren, saying El-Sayed’s comments had angered her because he did not know her son or “what type of person he is”.Aikins also defended Usha, calling her “one of the best, most genuine people” she had ever met and saying she loved the second lady “as if she were my own daughter”. She said El-Sayed’s comments about her grandchildren particularly upset her.“I’d probably punch the guy if I ever seen him, and then that would get me in trouble,” Aikins said, adding that she would instead “just go with the flow”.El-Sayed has repeatedly criticised Vance and his family. During an April podcast appearance, he referred to Vance’s children as “brown kids” while questioning whether the vice president’s political views were at odds with his children’s biracial background.He later appeared to reference Usha’s Indian heritage in a post on X after Vance invoked his late grandfather, writing: “So, do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no…”Vance subsequently hit back at El-Sayed during a rally for Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers in Michigan, telling him to keep his wife’s name “the hell out of your mouth”.El-Sayed is running as the Democratic candidate in the closely watched Michigan Senate race against Republican Mike Rogers.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Miami golfer Kai Trump opens up about emotional college transition
articles.summary: US News: Kai Trump, the 19-year-old granddaughter of US President Donald J. Trump, has opened up about the emotional challenges of leaving home and adjusting t.
articles.body: Kai Trump, the 19-year-old granddaughter of US President Donald J. Trump, has opened up about the emotional challenges of leaving home and adjusting to college life as she begins her freshman year with the University of Miami women's golf team.Trump documented her transition in a video posted to her YouTube channel, sharing her experience of moving from living with her mother to settling into an apartment as a university student. Her first week on campus was also complicated by illness after she developed strep throat.The teenager said leaving behind her family and friends had been more difficult than she anticipated, describing an emotional farewell before beginning her new chapter at university.“I’ve been, like, literally sobbing,” Trump said.She said saying goodbye to everyone had been particularly difficult, especially because she does not typically see herself as an emotional person.“It’s just, like, really sad that I have to say goodbye to, like, everyone today. I’m not, like, a very emotional person at all, so this is, like, really weird for me to cry,” she said.Trump also acknowledged that she was struggling with the transition despite being excited about starting college.“I’m just struggling right now, just, like, thinking about it, but, like, I’m excited,” Kai Trump said as she opened up about adjusting to college life.Her friend Emma also helped her settle into her new apartment. According to Trump, Emma picked up frozen food for her after she revealed that she had barely eaten for several days.“Emma got me some frozen foods because I haven’t eaten in like three days,” Kai said in the video.Her adjustment to university life was further disrupted when she fell ill during her first week. Trump said she was diagnosed with strep throat on Wednesday and returned home to Jupiter to recover.“I got sick with strep on Wednesday, my first week of school,” she said.“I came all the way back to Jupiter because I was so sick. I needed, like, my mom to nurse me back to health.”Trump has since appeared to recover and has shared official photographs from her first season with the University of Miami women's golf team on social media.“Year 1 ?? #gocanes,” she wrote on her Instagram handle.According to the reports given by thespun.com, Trump announced her commitment to the University of Miami women's golf programme two years ago. She is now entering her first season with the Hurricanes, marking the start of her college golf career alongside her transition to university life.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Priscilla Chan's grandfather died of cancer when she was in sixth grade; she found a cancer textbook and taught herself why he died
articles.summary: US News: Priscilla Chan was in sixth grade when the death of her grandfather from cancer changed the direction of her life. One morning, he dropped her off at .
articles.body: Priscilla Chan was in sixth grade when the death of her grandfather from cancer changed the direction of her life. One morning, he dropped her off at her sixth-grade classroom, but by the time she returned home, he had died. Chan was left trying to understand how someone who had taken her to school that morning could suddenly be gone. Science had always been her favourite subject, so she turned to it for answers. She bought an oncology textbook soon afterwards and began learning about cancer on her own. Years later, that childhood search for an explanation had evolved into a career in medicine and, eventually, a mission to accelerate biomedical research. As a paediatrician, Chan encountered children whose diseases medicine could not fully explain, reinforcing the same desire to understand disease that had first emerged after her grandfather's death.Priscilla Chan's search for answers began in sixth gradeChan has described losing her grandfather as the starting point of her journey into medicine. Her grandfather had been diagnosed with cancer, and according to a detailed Wall Street Journal profile, Chan accompanied him to medical appointments and helped translate for him. Her family had chosen not to tell him that he had cancer because they feared the knowledge could make him sicker. Then came the morning in sixth grade when he felt well enough to take Chan to school. By the time she came home, he had died. The suddenness of the loss left the young Chan asking what had happened. Rather than accepting that she could not understand it, she looked to the subject she trusted. In her own 2026 account, Chan recalled buying an oncology textbook because science had always been her favourite subject and she believed it might help her find answers. The episode is significant not because it proves that a single book determined her career, but because Chan herself identifies it as the beginning of her journey into medicine.She taught herself oncology from a cancer biology textbookChan's response to the loss was unusually academic for a child. Rather than simply reading about cancer out of curiosity, she used a textbook as a way of trying to make sense of something deeply personal. The Wall Street Journal profile says she found a cancer biology textbook on Amazon and devoured it, teaching herself the basics of oncology. Chan's own description is that she bought an oncology textbook because she thought science could help her find answers. That distinction is important. There is no credible evidence that the book allowed her to determine the precise medical circumstances of her grandfather's death, and available sources do not identify his particular type or stage of cancer. What the account does show is an early instinct that would remain central to Chan's later work: when confronted with something she did not understand, she wanted to investigate it. That habit of turning uncertainty into a scientific question would later become particularly important when she was caring for children with rare diseases for which even trained doctors had few answers.Her education took that curiosity from textbooks into medicineChan eventually turned that childhood curiosity into formal scientific and medical training. She became the first person in her family to attend college and studied biology at Harvard University. Before medical school, she spent a year teaching elementary school science, an experience that added another dimension to her interest in making scientific knowledge accessible. She then attended the University of California, San Francisco, where she earned her medical degree and completed her paediatrics residency. CZI's current biography describes her as a paediatrician whose direct experience caring for patients has shaped her commitment to accelerating scientific discovery. Her professional journey therefore gave her something the sixth-grade textbook could not: direct contact with patients, families and the practical limits of medical knowledge. The questions that had once been personal became professional ones. Instead of asking only why one family member had died, Chan began confronting the much broader problem of why doctors sometimes could not explain what was happening inside a sick child's body or provide an effective treatment.Treating children with rare diseases showed her the limits of medical knowledgeChan's years as a doctor brought her face-to-face with the unanswered questions that textbooks could not resolve. At UCSF, she worked with children with rare diseases, including patients referred to a national centre because their conditions were particularly difficult to diagnose or treat. Chan has recalled looking at a patient's diagnosis, searching the scientific literature and discovering that the medical community itself often had few answers. In some cases, she and her colleagues had to rely heavily on patients and their families to understand the condition because existing research was so limited. In a 2021 article, she described the difficulty of telling parents, after they had already spent months or years searching for help, that she did not know what was wrong with their child. She argued that this was precisely where better research could make a difference. Her experience also shaped her view of research as more than an academic exercise. For families dealing with rare disease, she came to see new scientific knowledge as a form of hope because a better understanding of biology can eventually lead to better diagnosis and treatment.The childhood question eventually became a mission to understand diseaseThat experience as a paediatrician helped shape the scientific direction of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, which Chan co-founded with Mark Zuckerberg. CZI says Chan now leads efforts to advance biomedical research and technology with the long-term goal of helping scientists cure, prevent or manage all disease by the end of this century. Its work has increasingly concentrated on the intersection of biology and artificial intelligence, including tools that could help researchers understand cells and the molecular mechanisms underlying disease. Chan has described this shift as deeply personal because her years as a doctor showed her how much remained unknown. In 2025, she wrote that working with children with rare diseases had exposed the limits of medicine and science and convinced her that expanding basic scientific knowledge was essential. CZI's current science programme includes AI-powered models and research tools intended to help scientists investigate human biology in ways that would be difficult or impossible using conventional approaches alone.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 11 death sentences, 19 life terms: Vietnam court’s massive verdict in drug case involving 227
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A court in Vietnam has sentenced 11 people to death and 19 others to life imprisonment in one of the country’s largest drug trafficking cases. A total.
articles.body: A court in Vietnam has sentenced 11 people to death and 19 others to life imprisonment in one of the country’s largest drug trafficking cases. A total of 227 defendants were convicted in a network that smuggled synthetic drugs from France, state media reported on Thursday.The Ho Chi Minh City People’s Court sentenced the 11 to death for illegal drug trafficking in the case known as VN10, according to VnExpress International. The alleged ringleader, who was tried in absentia, was among those given the death penalty.Local media reported that 227 people were sentenced in the case. Other defendants received punishments ranging from 18 months suspended imprisonment to 29 years in prison for offences including drug trafficking, drug sales and failing to report crimes.Authorities uncovered the network in early 2023 after customs officials at Ho Chi Minh City’s international airport found 11 kilograms of MDMA and ketamine concealed inside more than 150 toothpaste tubes, according to state media.The toothpaste tubes had been brought from France by four Vietnam Airlines flight attendants, who had agreed to transport what they believed were consumer goods, reports said.The attendants were not prosecuted after investigators found no evidence that they knew they were carrying drugs.According to state media, the ringleader organised multiple shipments of synthetic drugs concealed in toothpaste tubes and boxes of dietary supplements. He also recruited Vietnamese people studying or living in France to collect the drugs and send them to Vietnam through international express delivery services.The trial was conducted both in person and online because of the number of defendants and involved more than 120 lawyers, Tuoi Tre reported.Vietnam has some of the world’s strictest drug laws and routinely imposes the death penalty for serious drug offences. In 2024, 27 people were sentenced to death for trafficking more than 600 kilograms of drugs, including heroin, ketamine and methamphetamine, according to reports.Last year, 11 people, including two police officers, were sentenced to death for trafficking drugs from Laos.Vietnam has used lethal injection for executions since 2013, when it replaced firing squads.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Alan Carr lodges plans to turn Borders castle potting shed into café
articles.summary: The Celebrity Traitors winner bought 19th Century Ayton Castle earlier this year and will turn it into a home for his TV programme.
articles.body:
Comedian Alan Carr has lodged plans to convert a potting shed at his castle in the Scottish Borders into a cafe and estate shop.

A new TV series is planned following his attempt to turn the ageing estate into a workable home.

Now he has put in a planning application to Scottish Borders Council (SBC) to redevelop a part of the estate.

Inside the £3.25m castle bought by Celebrity Traitors winner Alan Carr

The castle was put up for sale with an asking price of offers over £3.25m before Carr snapped it up.

"Some men when they have a midlife crisis buy a Lamborghini or grow a ponytail, but me - I want my very own castle," he said at the time.

All of them found a buyer apart from a concrete cow.

Plans are in the pipeline for a Disney television series looking at his efforts to make the Scottish estate a workable home.

As a first step, a planning application has been submitted to the local council to convert some currently vacant buildings in its walled garden into a community cafe and estate shop.

It would include public toilets, staff welfare and storage facilities.

"With regard to the walled garden, there is a long-term commitment from the client to clear, repair and invest in this space over the coming years," said a heritage impact statement supporting the application.

It added that the potting sheds had sat vacant and were in a "severely derelict state" and any change which could bring them back into use and encourage people to visit would be a "highly positive development".

"For the portion that is to be converted into a cafe and shop, the dilapidated state means that any intervention is an improvement," the statement added.

"Overall, we objectively view that the proposed works will have minimal negative impact on the significance of the potting shed and as a whole provide a positive development in the life story of this single storey range of estate buildings.

"The proposal by our client to preserve and convert the potting sheds into a cafe and estate shop is both an appropriate change of use and one which meets all the basic principles of preservation, conservation and long-term sustainability while managing change in historic buildings."

SBC will decide at a later date if the plans should be allowed to proceed.

articles.title: Konda Surekha takes on CM Revanth Reddy, Congress after being removed from Telangana cabinet
articles.summary: HYDERABAD: Former Telangana minister Konda Surekha on Thursday questioned the decision to remove her from chief minister A Revanth Reddy’s cabinet, sa.
articles.body: HYDERABAD: Former Telangana minister Konda Surekha on Thursday questioned the decision to remove her from chief minister A Revanth Reddy’s cabinet, saying she had neither committed any corruption nor been given an opportunity to explain herself before the action was taken.Surekha said she had replied to the show-cause notices issued to her and questioned why she was not consulted before the decision to recommend her removal. She also questioned the authenticity of an unsigned communication announcing the action and said the move appeared to be an act of vendetta.Defending her daughter Konda Sushmitha Patel, whose remarks against Revanth Reddy and his family triggered the disciplinary row, Surekha said her daughter was an adult and her personal views could not be attributed to her.She questioned why she should be held responsible for comments made by her daughter and also asked what action had been taken against Congress leaders Komatireddy Raj Gopal Reddy and T Jagga Reddy when they had made controversial remarks.Surekha also questioned the decision to remove veteran Congress leader G Chinna Reddy as vice-chairman of the Telangana Planning Board, saying it was unfair to take action against him merely because disciplinary proceedings had been initiated against her.At the same time, Surekha welcomed the appointment of three BC women to key positions in the state, saying she was happy to see them being given important responsibilities.Asked about her political future, Surekha said she had not yet taken a decision and would decide on her next course of action.Surekha’s remarks came hours after Revanth Reddy recommended her removal from the Council of Ministers and decided to rescind Chinna Reddy’s appointment as vice-chairman of the Telangana Planning Board.The recommendation on Surekha’s removal was sent to governor Jishnu Dev Varma for approval, while Chinna Reddy’s removal was made effective immediately.The action followed recommendations by the Telangana Pradesh Congress Committee's (TPCC) disciplinary committee against both leaders over their recent remarks.The controversy involving Surekha intensified after her daughter made remarks against Revanth and his family at a public event last month. Surekha had maintained that her daughter’s comments were personal and that she should not be held responsible for them.The issue subsequently escalated within the Congress, with several leaders demanding action against Surekha. Revanth had also raised the matter with AICC general secretary KC Venugopal during his visit to Delhi and sought stringent action against her.Surekha had refused to resign despite mounting pressure and challenged the party leadership to take action against her. She also met Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge in Delhi on Wednesday as the high command considered disciplinary action.Chinna Reddy’s removal followed the disciplinary committee’s recommendation over his remarks against Wanaparthy MLA T Megha Reddy.Meanwhile, Revanth announced three appointments: Gadwal Vijayalakshmi as vice-chairperson of the Telangana Planning Board, Nerella Sharada as chairperson of the Telangana State Commission for Women and former Rajya Sabha MP G Sudha Rani as chairperson of the Kakatiya Urban Development Authority.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Hyderabad | Silver Rate in Hyderabad | Bank Holidays in Hyderabad | Public Holidays in Hyderabad | Hyderabad AQI | Weather in Hyderabad | Petrol Price in Hyderabad | Diesel Price in Hyderabad | CNG Price in Hyderabad | LPG Price in HyderabadStay updated with the latest Hyderabad news. articles.title: China’s grey-zone game: Why India must prepare for ‘armed coexistence’
articles.summary: India News: Former foreign secretary Vijay Gokhale argues that China waits for a strategic opening, acts pre-emptively and then builds a narrative of self-defence.
articles.body: Former foreign secretary Vijay Gokhale argues that China waits for a strategic opening, acts pre-emptively and then builds a narrative of self-defence.His new book, “China’s Wars: The Politics and Diplomacy Behind its Military Coercion”, examines past conflicts and China’s recent grey-zone tactics.In an interview with Indrajeet Rai, Gokhale explains why the India-China relationship has entered an era of “armed coexistence”, why a full-scale war is not the most likely outcome but cannot be ruled out, and how political uncertainty after Xi Jinping could produce global economic shocks or military adventurism. Edited excerpts:You describe China as an opportunistic power. What does that mean, and when does Beijing decide to act pre-emptively?By opportunistic power, I did not intend to suggest that China is very different from other major powers. In the case studies in my book, China waited for the international situation to turn favourable, or for some advantage to accrue from its relations with other major powers, before carrying out conflict with a neighbour or another country. It used opportunity strategically to achieve its goals.The Chinese idea of preventive deterrence or preventive conflict differs from the Western concept. In the West, deterrence is a counteraction intended to stop the adversary from escalating. In the Chinese context, it is pre-emptive: China acts even before the adversary has had the chance to act first. The aim is to deliver a political and psychological shock so the adversary desists or fears retaliation.The 1962 conflict is one example. There was no indication that India intended to launch a military assault. But China used the words of then PM Jawaharlal Nehru and an international situation dominated by the Cuban missile crisis to act pre-emptively against India.China often depicts its own aggressive action as defensive and blames the other side. How central is this narrative warfare to its strategy?The Chinese Communist Party utilised China’s difficult circumstances after the collapse of the empire and projected itself as the only organisation capable of pulling the country out of its problems. It placed the blame for China’s declining economy and global influence on external circumstances. It played the victim’s card: China was perennially the victim, and the party was the instrument that would restore it as a major power.The blame, therefore, was always placed on somebody else: The colonial powers, the United States in the Korean War, India in the 1962 war and the Soviet Union in the 1969 conflict. There was never an acknowledgement that some responsibility also fell on China.This is not limited to foreign policy. The party does not take responsibility for major domestic failures either: The Great Leap Forward, the Cultural Revolution or the 1989 Tiananmen incident. Blame falls on an external force or a few bad elements, never the party itself.You argue that China is pursuing sustained grey-zone coercion. How does this work against India?Since 1979, China has not fought a real conflict. The leadership made economic development the priority, and successive leaders after Mao Zedong focused on reform and opening up.But China was not willing to give up the use of force; it changed the manner in which force was used. Instead of hot wars or major conflict, it engaged and continues to engage in very low-intensity military conflict, popularly known as grey-zone warfare.Grey-zone warfare uses threats or actual force while staying below the threshold that might tempt the rival to launch a counteroffensive. It punishes or deters, but stops short of making the rival feel compelled to push back with force. We see it along the Line of Actual Control, in the South China Sea and in the East China Sea.I have characterised the situation on the LAC after 2020 as the end of peaceful coexistence and the beginning of armed coexistence. Armed coexistence does not mean conflict. It means China will continue to take grey-zone military action around the LAC to keep us tied down and to exhaust us not only financially - because keeping forces and equipment at those heights costs a lot - but also in terms of men and material.This fulfils a key Chinese objective: Keeping India confined to South Asia.Apart from the United States, there are few potential rivals in this century, and India is one. If you look at India, it's geographical location, its population size, its territorial size, its talent, it's economic potential. All of it lends a credence to the belief that India can become a major power in this century. And clearly, China would like to delay that possibility.Does that mean a large-scale India-China war is unlikely in the foreseeable future?Nobody can predict this definitively. China and its decision-making processes are opaque, and there are no alternative channels of information such as free media or civil society.China is a mature state focused on becoming the strongest economy and power in the world. On a rational cost-benefit analysis, the price of a major war with India could exceed the benefits. Logically, China would be reluctant to engage in such a conflict.At the end of the day, however, it is impossible to predict. We have to be prepared for the worst, while logically understanding that a hot conflict with India may not be in China’s interest in the foreseeable future.China’s capabilities against Taiwan have grown, while the US is distracted by several conflicts. Could Xi Jinping move on Taiwan to secure his legacy?An American commander of the Indo-Pacific Command, Admiral Philip Davidson, suggested that by 2027 China would have the military capability to launch an assault on Taiwan. Some interpreted that to mean China would attack by 2027, but he did not actually say this.China’s capabilities for an assault on an island have substantially increased: Landing craft, area-denial capabilities, communication systems and anti-ship missiles.It is one thing for a major power to bomb another country and destroy its infrastructure, and quite another to occupy or conquer it. That requires a very large commitment of forces and material, with no assured guarantee of victory.China’s demographic decline is already causing anxiety. An assault would mean mass casualties because boots on the ground would be required. After Galwan, India acknowledged within days that 20 soldiers had been martyred; China took much longer to admit fatalities. With Taiwan potentially producing casualties in the hundreds or thousands, Beijing will worry about the domestic impact.This is where democracy, for all its weaknesses, becomes a strength. A democratic government has electoral and constitutional legitimacy to act, including in war. In China, the party claims it has popular support but has never tested that proposition. The reaction to large-scale war casualties is unpredictable.Xi has removed the age and term limits that helped institutionalise succession. What happens after him and why should India worry?Deng Xiaoping introduced two reforms that stabilised succession: Those above 68 could not continue in top party positions, and the president was limited to two five-year terms. This helped ensure smooth transitions from Jiang Zemin to Hu Jintao and then to Xi Jinping.Xi has abolished the age and term limits. In an authoritarian system, no leader will voluntarily give up power because enemies may find it easier to target him, and he cannot be certain a successor will not misuse authority against him.China could enter a period of political uncertainty and potentially turmoil as Xi ages and factions emerge in a contest for power. It is unclear whether this happens before or after his death, or whether he intends to stand for a fourth term.Because China is the world’s second-largest economy, domestic turmoil would affect its economy, military and diplomacy and create huge ripple effects abroad. Beleaguered regimes also sometimes use an external threat to divert attention. India must consider whether turmoil could produce military adventurism and how to preserve its national interests, sovereignty and territorial integrity.China has few formal allies and did little visibly to support Iran. Does it lack the partnerships needed to become a global leader?China lacks the United States’ large network of treaty allies. But we should not underestimate the goodwill it enjoys. The Belt and Road Initiative has been welcomed as an alternative route to development. Western assistance often came with harsh conditions; China offers fewer and less onerous strings. Nobody gives aid for free, but China has built substantial diplomatic influence.There was little need for China to do more in the Iran war. It could neither persuade the United States to stop nor force peace. It protected its oil interests and relations with Iran and the Gulf countries without entering the mediation game.When the conflict ends, Iran will rebuild using its oil and gas wealth. It is unlikely to trust the West, while China can build infrastructure at a scale few others can match. China needs energy; Iran needs infrastructure and money. That creates an enormous downstream economic opportunity and a win-win situation. Why would China get significantly involved now when there seems to be no clear way out of the conflict?As US-China rivalry intensifies, which side of the emerging world order should India prefer?India should not look at the world order through an either-or lens. The United States and China will both remain major powers. The question is how, in a triangular or quadrangular relationship, including the European Union if it acts as a union, we create an international framework relevant to this century.India has objective advantages: Its location, demographics and consumer base; tested political stability; an independent military capability and growing defence industry; and talent.I do not see how India can fail to become a major power in this century. The international order is disintegrating and all states are hedging their bets; India is doing so too. The task is not to choose a US-led or China-led order. It is to help build an order in which India is one of the leaders.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Andy Burnham praises UK-EU ties in meeting with Emmanuel Macron
articles.summary: The pair are discussing small boats, defence and Ukraine in Burnham's first bilateral talks in Downing Street.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has praised the UK-EU relationship as he holds talks with French President Emmanuel Macron about issues such as small boat crossings in the English Channel and defence.

The pair shook hands and posed for photographs alongside their wives outside 10 Downing Street on Thursday morning.

They are discussing "shared challenges" including the rise of "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally, which the Conservatives say shows the UK government has failed to "smash the gangs".

Burnham said it was "so fitting" that Macron was his first overseas visitor in Downing Street since becoming PM in July, describing him as "our nearest neighbour and close friend Emmanuel".

"It shows what collaboration can achieve, just as we are also showing on Ukraine, on small boats, and also on strengthening the UK-EU relationship. So I look forward to discussing those themes further with you today," Burnham added.

Macron's visit to the UK was primarily to mark the Bayeux Tapestry's loan to the British Museum . The French leader met King Charles at the museum on Wednesday, ahead of the medieval tapestry going on public display next week.

In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron are discussing not just small boats but also the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as defence and EU co-operation.

But the "mega dinghies" crossing the Channel illegally - first seen earlier in August with a 15-metre long vessel carrying a record 230 migrants towards the UK - are arguably the most pressing challenge facing the pair.

It follows a summer when the overall number of small boat arrivals in the UK fell to a seven-year low.

Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them.

Earlier on Tuesday, Home Office Minister Anna Turley said the officers were "just part of the armoury" of more than 1,000 officers on northern French beaches who are now doing "actual intervention" in the water.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that videos in recent weeks "show them going to the boats, slashing them, pushing people back, being bombarded with stones and bricks and coming under a lot of challenge to do that, so they are intervening".

In a post on X , in which he said he was "do[ing] politics differently", Burnham laid out the latest small boat, returns and asylum hotel figures, describing smuggling gangs as a "shared European challenge".

Asked about the extra police on French beaches, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch told the BBC she welcomed European collaboration "but the boats aren't stopping".

"We have spent hundreds of millions, if not billions, paying the French to man the borders," she said.

articles.title: Liechtenstein MPs vote to legalise abortion despite threat of veto
articles.summary: Organisers of the citizens' initiative say they have popular support, even though the all-powerful monarch has said he will veto the legislation.
articles.body:
Liechtenstein's parliament has narrowly backed a citizens' initiative to legalise abortion during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

The initiative, led by a group of women, would also lift a nationwide ban on providing information about abortions and make the procedure eligible for health insurance.

It was approved by 13 votes to 12 in the 25-seat parliament. However, it is unlikely to become law as the country's all-powerful ruler, Hereditary Prince Alois, has previously said he will veto the legislation.

Supporters of the bill say there is widespread backing in Liechtenstein to legalise abortion. However, MPs rejected a separate proposal to put the issue to a public vote.

Almost 80% of Liechtenstein's population of about 41,000 people belong to the Roman Catholic Church which is opposed to abortion.

The country last held a referendum on legalising abortion in 2011, when the proposal was rejected by 52% of voters. Hereditary Prince Alois had indicated at the time that he would have opposed the change.

In Liechtenstein, it is allowed only in limited circumstances, including when a woman's life is at risk or a pregnancy is the result of rape.

Anyone who carries out an abortion outside those exceptions can face up to three years in prison, while a woman undergoing the procedure can be jailed for up to a year.

The current restrictions mean women have to go to other countries - mainly neighbouring Austria and Switzerland - to have an abortion. Since 2015, they have been able to do so without facing a penalty, but the cost is not covered by the health insurance.

The initiative to change the law was led by 28-year-old Tatjana As'Ad of the small left-wing Free List party. Supporters collected 4,970 signatures, nearly five times over the threshold needed to bring the proposal before parliament.

The proposed 12-week limit is already used in many European countries. In England, Scotland and Wales, it is legally available up to 23 weeks and six days under most circumstances.

However, some lawmakers had argued that there was little point taking the initiative further because of the monarch's opposition.

The Princely House has said its main concern with the initiative is that it does not provide enough protection for unborn life.

Hereditary Prince Alois has, however, suggested that changes could be made to the current rules, including lifting restrictions on public information and clarifying existing regulations.

He carries out public duties on behalf of his father, Prince Hans-Adam, and has unusually wide powers for a Western European monarch - including dismissing the government or individual ministers, appointing judges and proposing changes to the law, in addition to vetoing legislation.

articles.title: MG Alba boss says Gaelic media services lack funding
articles.summary: John Morrison says Irish and Welsh services receive millions of pounds of public money.
articles.body:
The chairman of MG Alba has told MPs that Gaelic media services have missed out on "serious" public funding.

MG Alba services include the LearnGaelic website and it works with the BBC to deliver Gaelic language service BBC Alba.

John Morrison told the Scottish Affairs Committee's inquiry into the future of Gaelic broadcasting that Welsh and Irish services receive "millions of pounds" to help them diversify.

The Scottish government, which provided £15m to MG Alba for 2026-27, said the organisation did not benefit from "fair funding" direct from the TV licence fee.

Highland Council seek views on 'areas of linguistic significance'

Gaelic initiative focuses on creating jobs in language's heartlands

Morrison said MG Alba's work encouraged the growth of Gaelic, particularly among young people.

"The most important thing for us is not MG Alba, it's not BBC Alba, it's about the whole language and the importance of the language to the increasing number of young people who are embracing it," he said.

Morrison, a former BBC News correspondent, added: "We are no longer a linear TV channel. We are having to work on multiple platforms.

"Our colleagues in the Celtic countries got serious millions of pounds of support to help them diversify, or the 'dash to digital' as we call it.

"We got no money to support us with that."

In a written submission to the inquiry , MG Alba said it received £15m from the Scottish government and a £10m allocation for content from the BBC.

It said S4C in Wales received £22m worth of content from the BBC, plus licence fee funding of £95m.

MG Alba said Irish language public service broadcaster TG4 was also "significantly better funded", and also benefitted from tax-based incentives.

Gaelic Secretary Màiri McAllan said the BBC had a responsibility to Scottish licence payers to commission, invest in and broadcast programming which reflected people's lives in Scotland - including Gaelic language and culture.

She added: "Unlike S4C in Wales, MG ALBA does not receive direct funding from the licence fee.

"We continue to call on the UK government to ensure fair funding from the licence fee as part of the BBC Charter renewal process."

The UK government is reviewing the charter ahead of the current term expiring on 31 December 31 2027, with the new charter set to take effect on 1 January 2028.

BBC Alba was set up in 2008 and broadcasts news and current affairs, sport, drama and children's programmes.

The channel had nightly live coverage and highlights throughout the Glasgow 2026 Commonwealth Games, while An t-Eilean (The Island) was the most high-profile drama in BBC Alba's history .

articles.title: 'Why should I even respond to this?': Aaditya Thackeray on Disha Salian case after HC orders CBI probe
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray on Thursday dismissed allegations linking him to the death of celebrity manager Disha Salian, ques.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Aaditya Thackeray on Thursday dismissed allegations linking him to the death of celebrity manager Disha Salian, questioning why he should respond to them. His remarks came after the Bombay high court directed the CBI to probe Salian’s death.Speaking to reporters, Aaditya Thackeray, the son of former Maharashtra chief minister Uddhav Thackeray said, "It's something that I have nothing to do about and not even thought about. Why should I even respond to this? BJP tries to defame everybody. They have tried to make Rahul Gandhi a 'Pappu' for years.”“They have tried to defame me for the last six years. Anybody who pricks the BJP, they have a problem with them. Like I said, when you have nothing to do with anything, why speak on anything or give it any importance? That's my stand..." he added.Earlier in the day, Maharashtra minister Nitesh Rane said that if Thackeray and others named in connection with the case had nothing to do with Salian’s death, they should come forward and clarify their position.Rane said he had maintained from the beginning that Salian’s death should not be treated as a suicide and expressed confidence that the CBI investigation would establish the facts."We were clear from day one that this was not a suicide; this was a murder case. And events of that nature are now coming to light. Now the CBI investigation will begin, and an FIR will be lodged," Rane said.He said he expected the probe to examine allegations of evidence being destroyed and misuse of power."My only expectation is that regarding the wrong that was done to our sister named Disha Salian—the way power was misused to destroy evidence and proof—all of those things are now going to come out. In the end, no matter how much you try to hide the truth, it eventually comes out," he added.Bombay HC orders CBI probeThe remarks came after the Bombay high court directed the CBI to register an FIR and conduct a thorough investigation into the circumstances surrounding Salian’s death. The court also directed Malvani Police Station to hand over relevant records to the CBI.The high court said no person should be treated as an accused merely on the basis of allegations made before the court.“Nobody shall be treated as an accused unless in the opinion of the investigating officer there are sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against him depending on the material collected during the investigation,” the court said.The CBI has been asked to appoint a suitably experienced and senior officer to conduct the investigation.The court also said that if the probe finds that no criminal case has been made out, the CBI must file an appropriate summary report before the competent court.“In case the investigation reveals that no case is made out, then the CBI shall file the appropriate summary report before the court concerned,” it said.Salian’s father, Satish Salian, would be free to challenge such a report and file objections before the court.The high court had earlier raised concerns over the registration of only an Accidental Death Report (ADR), instead of an FIR, despite allegations made by Salian’s family. It also noted that copies of the post-mortem report and ADR had not been provided to the family even years after her death.Advocate Nilesh Ojha, who represented Satish Salian, said the court had directed the CBI to record his statement and appoint a senior officer to investigate the case.The court described Salian’s father as an “unfortunate” parent who had lost his young daughter in “tragic circumstances” and said the matter required a substantive investigation. However, it did not make any adverse finding against any individual named in the allegations.Thackeray had separately approached the high court seeking to intervene in the proceedings. In his application, he described Satish Salian’s petition as “false, frivolous and motivated” and sought an opportunity to be heard before any order was passed.Salian, a celebrity manager, was found dead on June 8, 2020, after falling from a building in Mumbai. Her death occurred days before actor Sushant Singh Rajput was found dead at his Bandra residence.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.body: Maya Higa recently had an awkward phone call with streamer Stable Ronaldo after he called to congratulate her on her engagement to her longtime partner, Caleb. articles.title: US woman's family joked about her looking 'nothing' like her siblings, then a DNA test revealed something even more shocking
articles.summary: US News: Every child grows up believing that they are an indispensable part of their family. Yet every sibling also grows up hearing how they are apparently ad.
articles.body: Every child grows up believing that they are an indispensable part of their family. Yet every sibling also grows up hearing how they are apparently adopted. Payton Lee's siblings often joked about how she didn't look like her four younger siblings. A running family joke led to a DNA test that suddenly transformed the joke into a reality. “The idea that I have a different dad than my four younger siblings had honestly never crossed my mind until a few months ago,” Payton told PEOPLE. “I had always just thought none of us looked alike.”The joke began after Payton returned to her hometown and her brother mentioned that her siblings had been talking about how little she resembled them. Initially, she laughed it off, but when she began comparing old baby photos, she noticed how her siblings and her nephew looked alike, but she didn't.For the first time ever, the 29-year-old began wondering if the joke could be a reality. She likely would have left the thought alone, but her mother-in-law surprised her and her youngest sister with DNA tests. “I don’t think I ever would have bought or taken one if it was up to me,” she says. “One of the hardest parts of all of this has been that I never really made the choice to take that test, so I wasn’t emotionally prepared for what it could actually uncover.”When the results arrived, Payton was out of town, and her siblings gathered at her sister's house to open them together while she was on FaceTime. She saw it first: the sister she had always believed was her full sister was listed as her half-sister. Then Payton kept looking, and the discovery got bigger. Directly below her sister’s name was another half-sister, someone Payton had never heard of, making it clear that the biological relatives appearing on her paternal side belonged to an entirely different family.“That’s when it really hit me that the people on my father’s side were a completely different family,” she recalled. The result also meant something even harder to absorb: the man Payton had called Dad for 29 years was not her biological father.When she FaceTimed her dad to tell him the results, he didn't believe it at first. “He made it very clear that this doesn’t change anything and I’m still his daughter!” she said. For her, her dad had always been the fun parent, the one who took them all for outings and trips and filled their childhood with happy memories. After learning that her mother had been about six months pregnant with Payton when her parents married, however, Payton found herself thinking about the discovery from his perspective, too. “I honestly felt really bad knowing that he entered that marriage believing I was his biological child,” she said.“He has had such a great attitude about everything and hasn’t held any resentment or been angry, which I don’t know if I would be able to do if I were in his shoes!” she said.For Payton, the experience also changed her thoughts about DNA testing at home, when one is expecting nothing more than just fun. “So take it from me,” Payton said, “DNA tests should never be taken lightly!”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Pro-Israel activist Stephanie Benshimol confronted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a visit to a Jewish store in Brooklyn’s Borough Park ahead of Rosh Hashanah.According to the New York Post, Benshimol, a self-described “American Israeli Zionist” and founder of United Zionists, accused Mamdani of fueling antisemitism in the city and questioned his decision to visit the heavily Jewish neighbourhood.“Shame on you, you’re causing all the antisemitism,” Benshimol was heard saying while filming the encounter inside Eichler’s Judaica store.Benshimol, who has described herself as a granddaughter of Holocaust survivors, also invoked her family’s connection to Borough Park while confronting the mayor.“My Bubbie and Zaidy came to Borough Park! During his visit, he said it was “so great to be here before the holidays” and wished people a happy new year, while thanking them for the “welcome and the dialogue.”The confrontation comes amid heightened debate over antisemitism in New York City, with NYPD data showing hate crimes had risen citywide this year and antisemitic incidents accounting for a majority of reported hate crimes.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body:
A large pharmaceutical warehouse in Boryspil near Kiev was damaged in a Russian airstrike, one person was injured, and the facility was one of the largest specialized pharmaceutical warehouses in Ukraine.

The Russian military has increased attacks on various distribution centers in Ukraine, including food, cold-storage facilities, online retailers' shipping hubs, and DIY stores, while Ukraine has targeted distribution centers of Russian online retail giants Wildberries and Ozon.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that 13 regions were affected by Russian airstrikes overnight, with 17 people injured in Odessa when a drone struck a high-rise building, leading to continuous air raid alerts due to the threat of Russian jet-powered drone attacks.

A large pharmaceutical warehouse in the Ukrainian city of Boryspil near Kiev was damaged in a Russian airstrike on Thursday, according to media reports.

The Ukrainska Pravda news outlet said the facility was one of the largest specialized pharmaceutical warehouses in Ukraine.

Kiev regional military governor Tymur Tkachenko confirmed only that a warehouse had been hit but, as is customary, provided no further details. One person was injured, he said on Telegram.

The Russian military has stepped up attacks on distribution centres for food, cold-storage facilities, online retailers' shipping hubs and DIY stores in Ukraine.

Ukraine, for its part, has attacked numerous distribution centres belonging to Russian online retail giants Wildberries and Ozon.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said 13 regions had been affected by Russian airstrikes overnight.

In Odessa, 17 people were injured when a drone struck a high-rise building, he said.

"In many cities and communities, air raid alerts practically do not stop because of the threat of Russian jet-powered drone attacks," Zelensky wrote on social media.

Ukraine is in the fifth year of defending itself against Russia's full-scale invasion. Efforts to end the war have stalled as Moscow continues to pursue its goal of subjugating its neighbour.
